Fine Flour
FINE FLOWR
noun
The KJV rendering of Hebrew sōleth, the finest wheaten meal, sifted free of bran and coarseness; the appointed substance of the meat (meal) offering.

Biblical Definition

Fine flour is the finest wheaten meal, ground small and sifted clean, and it is the appointed matter of the meat offering — the meal offering of the sanctuary: “when any will offer a meat offering unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon” (Lev 2:1). It was no coarse or common meal, but flour without lump or grit, evenly milled to a uniform sweetness. It accompanied the daily lamb (Exo 29:40) and filled the silver chargers of the princes’ offering, “full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering” (Num 7:13). The meat offering had no blood; it was the offering of a life given wholly to God in unbroken obedience, and its substance preaches Christ. He is the true fine flour — a manhood perfectly even, no coarse grain of sin, no lump of self-will, ground small in suffering yet sifted clean, of one uniform holiness throughout. The oil poured on Him is the anointing Spirit; the frankincense is the sweet savour of His life Godward. Yet the same fine flour is found in the merchandise of fallen Babylon (Rev 18:13), traded as a luxury with the souls of men — a warning that what God appointed for pure worship the world will always seek to buy and sell. In the sanctuary it is Christ offered; in Babylon it is Christ made merchandise.

Webster 1828 Definition

The finest sifted wheaten meal, the matter of the meat offering, figuring Christ’s evenly perfect and sinless manhood offered to God.

FINE FLOUR, the finest wheaten meal, ground small and sifted free of coarseness.

The appointed substance of the meat (meal) offering (Lev 2:1).

Poured with oil and set with frankincense as a sweet savour.

Accompanied the daily lamb and filled the princes’ chargers (Exo 29:40; Num 7:13).

A figure of Christ’s even, sinless manhood offered wholly to God.

Key Scripture

Lev 2:1 — "And when any will offer a meat offering unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon:"

Exo 29:40 — "And with the one lamb a tenth deal of flour mingled with the fourth part of an hin of beaten oil; and the fourth part of an hin of wine for a drink offering."

Num 7:13 — "And his offering was one silver charger, the weight thereof was an hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary; both of them were full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering:"

Rev 18:13 — "And cinnamon, and odours, and ointments, and frankincense, and wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, and beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men."

Modern Corruption

Not a doctrine in dispute but a sifted meal, fine flour recovers the evenness of Christ’s holy manhood — and warns against making Him merchandise.

expand to see more

The temptation fine flour rebukes is the tolerance of coarseness — the age’s ease with a lumpy, half-sifted holiness, a self-will left in the meal, a grit of sin unground. The meat offering would have nothing coarse in it; God’s eye passed over every particle. But there is a second and sharper corruption, named plainly in Babylon’s cargo, where fine flour is sold for gain alongside the souls of men — the making of holy things into merchandise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the even, entire holiness of Christ, the true fine flour, ground small in His sufferings yet sifted of all sin, of one uniform sweetness throughout. Let the worshipper bring nothing coarse to God, and let the church beware Babylon’s traffic, which prices what heaven appointed for pure worship. In the sanctuary the fine flour is Christ offered; in Babylon it is Christ made merchandise.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for the finest sifted meal, fine flour is the matter of the meat offering, a figure of the evenly holy manhood of Christ.
